section.title: Continuity
section.p: The precise definition of a limit gave us a way to control nearby values: x\text{ close to }a \implies f(x)\text{ close to }L. But a limit does not care about the value at the point itself. A function may have a hole, a wrong value, or no value at all, and still have a limit nearby.
Continuity is the calm case: nearby behavior and the actual value agree.

subsection.title: Continuity at a point
subsection.p: Recall F(x)=2x+1 for x\neq 1 and F(1)=-1. Here \lim_{x\to 1}F(x)=3, but F(1)=-1. The limit exists, but does not match the actual value. This function is not continuous at x=1.

statement.p: A function f is continuous at a if
For f(x)=x^2 at x=2, f(2)=4 and \lim_{x\to 2}x^2=4. Since \lim_{x\to 2}f(x)=f(2), x^2 is continuous at 2. Because this holds for every real number a, x^2 is continuous everywhere.

paragraphs.title: The \varepsilon-\delta version of continuity
paragraphs.p: A function f is continuous at a if, for every \varepsilon\gt 0, there is a \delta\gt 0 such that whenever |x-a|\lt \delta, we have |f(x)-f(a)|\lt \varepsilon.
Notice that continuity uses the full interval |x-a|\lt \delta rather than the punctured interval 0\lt |x-a|\lt \delta.

subsection.title: Holes and continuous extensions
subsection.p: Consider g(x)=\frac{x^2-1}{x-1} for x\neq 1. While \lim_{x\to 1}g(x)=2, g(1) is undefined, so g is not continuous at 1.

The function q(x)=\sqrt{1+x^2} is continuous everywhere because 1+x^2\ge 1 is continuous and \sqrt{u} is continuous for u\ge 0. Therefore \lim_{x\to 3}\sqrt{1+x^2}=\sqrt{1+3^2}=\sqrt{10}.
The function r(x)=\sin(x^2) is continuous everywhere because x^2 and \sin u are continuous everywhere. Thus \lim_{x\to a}\sin(x^2)=\sin(a^2).

subsection.title: A continuity checklist

row.cell: If not, the function is not continuous at a.
If one-sided limits disagree or values explode, it is not continuous at a.
If not, nearby behavior and the actual value disagree.

subsection.p: Continuity is a local property near a point, but it has powerful global consequences: a continuous function on a closed interval cannot skip intermediate values and must reach an absolute maximum and minimum. These theorems are the focus of the next section.
